events.title: A rover mission reaches Mars
events.description: Pathfinder lands carrying the small Sojourner rover.

events.title: The euro begins
events.description: Eleven countries start sharing a currency for financial transactions. Euro notes and coins will arrive later.

events.title: The September 11 attacks
events.description: Terrorist attacks kill thousands of people in the United States. Families, communities and rescuers face devastating losses.

what_happened_next.text:
Microsoft more than tripled, while Nike lost about one-fifth of its value. Apple gained overall but suffered a fall of more than half in one month during the window. The US basket gained more steadily than that single share, though it also fell sharply at times. The ending number alone leaves out much of the experience.

Pathfinder reached Mars in 1997, and the euro began for financial transactions in 1999. The September 11 attacks occurred in the last month of this window, bringing devastating losses to families and communities. These are important parts of the history, rather than simple explanations for every movement in the chart.

Apple’s positive final return is worth comparing with its severe fall along the way. A fall of half turns $100 into $50; it then takes a doubling to get back to $100. That uneven math is one reason the route matters. An investor who needed to use the money during a low point would have had a different experience from someone able to wait.

reflection.what_people_were_focused_on: Investors compared famous fund managers with indexes. Computer competition, an internet attack and Tiger Woods’s professional debut also drew attention.
reflection.what_actually_mattered: The route to the final value mattered. A positive five-year total could include losses that would have been hard to sit through.
reflection.what_faded_away: An athlete’s promising career did not guarantee a rising sponsor’s share price. The most popular investment manager was not automatically the best choice either.
reflection.what_nobody_knew: The exact technology-stock reversals and the September 11 attacks were unknown. No confident starting story removed those risks.

hot_stock_outcomes.text: Nike’s fast growth hit problems. The Asian financial crisis and weaker U.S. demand left too many shoes to sell in 1998, forcing discounts. In 2001, a new planning system left Nike with too much of some products and too little of others. U.S. shoe sales fell about 4% that year. These setbacks help explain the disappointing stock result.

Steve Jobs returned when Apple bought NeXT in 1997. Apple simplified its products and launched the iMac in 1998, returning to a $309 million annual profit. The recovery was uneven: too many unsold computers helped produce a $195 million loss in the 2000 holiday quarter. Apple finished this window ahead, but the turnaround still had serious setbacks.

Office 97 and Windows NT sold strongly, and Windows 98 arrived in 1998. Microsoft’s annual sales climbed from $14.48 billion in June 1998 to $25.30 billion in June 2001. Businesses adopted Windows 2000, and Office XP launched in May 2001. This expanding software business helped the shares finish well ahead, despite the technology-stock slump near the end.
